title: Chenuli Muthukuda Arachchige
text:
Hi, I’m Chenuli! I’m currently a first-year Master of Business Analytics student at Monash University in Melbourne.
I completed my Bachelor of Business and Commerce at Monash University Malaysia, majoring in International Business Management, with minors in marketing and management. That degree gave me a strong understanding of how organisations, markets and people work, and taught me that good decisions depend on information people can actually understand and use.
In my Masters, I’m building the technical side of that: working with R, cleaning and analysing data, statistical modelling, and turning results into clear visualisations and reports.
I’m open to opportunities in business analytics and data-driven roles, especially where data can help organisations make better decisions.
Having a multicultural background and studying in different countries has shaped how I see the world and how I connect with people from different backgrounds. It has also given me a love of travelling and experiencing new cultures.

title: Climate change has nearly doubled the chance of Black Summer-level fire weather
text: In southeastern Australia, the extreme fire weather behind the 2019–20 Black Summer bushfires is no longer as rare as it once was. Climate models show the chance of it happening in any given year has risen since the early 1900s, to about 1.8 times what it was then. If global warming reaches 2°C, that chance could rise to about eight times the early-1900s level (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).

title: Climate change has nearly doubled the chance of Black Summer-level fire weather
section: Black Summer showed how dangerous extreme fire weather can be
text:
Black Summer showed how dangerous extreme fire weather can be
Black Summer burned more land near towns and cities than any bushfire season before it. Between late 2019 and January 2020, the fires killed at least 34 people, destroyed about 5,900 buildings and burned at least 19.4 million hectares (Oldenborgh et al. 2021). They followed Australia’s hottest and driest year on record (Bureau of Meteorology 2020).
For anyone living near the bush, those fires raise an unsettling question: was Black Summer a once-in-a-lifetime disaster, or a sign of things to come? Answering that question means asking two things: is fire weather this extreme becoming more common, and what is driving it?
A team of 17 researchers set out to find out (Oldenborgh et al. 2021). They focused on southeastern Australia, where the fires were particularly severe. They then compared two periods: today, and the early 1900s, before most human-caused warming. For each, they estimated the chance of Black Summer-level fire weather happening in any given year.
By “fire weather”, the researchers mean the weather conditions that make bushfires more dangerous: heat, dry air, wind and a lack of rain. They looked only at the weather, not at how fires start or how much bush there is to burn.
The researchers report their results as “times as likely”. For example, if Black Summer-level fire weather were twice as likely, you could expect a season like it twice as often as in the early 1900s. The rest of this post looks at how much more likely this fire weather has become, what is driving the change, and what it means for you.

title: Climate change has nearly doubled the chance of Black Summer-level fire weather
section: Dangerous fire weather is already more likely than a century ago
text:
Dangerous fire weather is already more likely than a century ago








Figure 1: The chance of fire weather as extreme as Black Summer (2019–20) is already higher than in the early 1900s, and could become about eight times higher if the world warms by 2°C. Each estimate compares the chance of this kind of fire weather happening in southeastern Australia in any given year with the chance in the early 1900s. The dashed line (1×) marks the same chance as back then. Filled dots show the best estimate and open circles show the lowest likely value. Real weather records only give a lowest likely value, so the true figure could be higher. Data: Oldenborgh et al. (2021).

title: Climate change has nearly doubled the chance of Black Summer-level fire weather
section: Rising heat is doing most of the work

Rising heat is doing most of the work




Table 1: Heat is the main reason fire weather has become more dangerous, while rainfall shows no long-term climate change trend. The number columns show how important each weather ingredient is as a cause of the rise in fire danger. Data: van Oldenborgh et al. (2021).
